name: One-pan salmon rice with soy & spring onion (אורז עם סלמון במחבת)

source.author: Pasted recipe (Hebrew)
source.notes: One-pan dish: salmon seared skin-down until crispy and set aside, rice toasted in the same pan, cooked with water + soy + garlic + salt with the salmon laid on top, rested covered, then the salmon flaked in with lots of spring onion, sesame oil and sesame seeds. Analyzed as 4 servings; 'lots of spring onion' taken as ~60 g, salmon as 350 g (mid of 300–400 g, farmed Atlantic, skin on), white rice (type not specified), ~1 tbsp searing oil and ~1 tbsp sesame seeds. Manual intake — kept as reference, not adopted. Estimate.

ingredients.note: the dish's main calorie source — see mods

steps: Sear the salmon skin-side down in a little oil until the skin is crispy, flip and sear the other side; remove when almost cooked.
Toast the rinsed rice in the same pan 1–2 min.
Add the water, soy sauce, garlic and a little salt and stir.
Lay the salmon on the rice, cover, bring to a boil on medium, then cook on low 12–15 min.
Turn off the heat and leave covered 10 more min.
Flake the salmon, add plenty of spring onion, sesame oil and sesame seeds, and mix. Keep the crispy skin on top or remove it, as you like.

batch_totals.note: Whole pan (4 servings). The ratio is rice-heavy: 2 cups of dry rice supplies over half the calories and almost all the carbs, while 350 g of salmon split four ways gives only ~26 g protein per serving. Fat is mostly salmon (good omega-3) plus the searing and sesame oils.

him.verdict: Great ingredients — salmon brings ~1.6 g omega-3 and ~450 IU vitamin D per serving (two of your sperm-priority micros) — but the proportions work against a cut. Two cups of dry rice for 350 g of salmon makes this a carb-led dish: ~605 kcal and ~77 g carbs for only ~26 g protein (~4.3 g protein per 100 kcal, low for your library). It's easy to fix by changing the rice-to-salmon ratio rather than the recipe itself.
flags: ~1.6 g omega-3 + ~450 IU vitamin D per serving (sperm micros)
rice-heavy ratio: ~77 g carbs vs ~26 g protein per serving
~4.3 g protein per 100 kcal — low for this library
moderate-high sodium (~830 mg) from 3 tbsp soy
suggested_mods: Flip the ratio: 1 cup rice + 500–600 g salmon (water down to ~1½ cups) — roughly doubles protein per serving
Use brown rice (longer cook, a bit more water) or mix in edamame/peas for fibre
Low-sodium soy, and skip the added salt
Halve the sesame oil — the seeds and spring onion carry the flavour

her_preconception.verdict: Very good for her: salmon is low-mercury and one of the best DHA + vitamin D sources, and the dish is fully cooked through by steaming on the rice. It isn't a folate or iron source, so pair it with greens. Just make sure the salmon is opaque and flakes easily before eating.
prenatal_highlights: DHA/omega-3 + vitamin D (salmon) — fetal brain development
low-mercury fish; fully cooked; selenium + B12

safety_advisories.note: Salmon is pulled 'almost cooked' and finishes steaming on the rice — check it's fully opaque and flakes before serving.
safety_advisories.swap: give it a few extra minutes covered if the centre is still translucent

suggested_mods: Serve with a green vegetable side for folate and vitamin C

cooking_guide: Pat the salmon skin completely dry and start it skin-down in a hot, lightly oiled pan; press gently for the first 30 sec so the skin stays flat and crisps evenly. Don't move it until it releases on its own.
Pull the salmon while the centre is still slightly translucent — it finishes cooking as it steams on top of the rice, so fully cooking it now makes it dry.
Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, and drain well before toasting — this keeps the grains separate instead of gluey.
Toast the rice in the salmon fat 1–2 min to pick up flavour from the pan.
Once it boils, drop to the lowest heat and don't lift the lid — the trapped steam cooks the rice and the salmon together.
Don't skip the 10-minute covered rest off the heat; it finishes the rice and lets the moisture even out.
Add the spring onion, sesame oil and sesame only at the end so they stay fresh and fragrant. If you keep the skin, lay it on top just before serving so it stays crisp.
